History & Physical (Super Detailed)

Consult Summary:
66-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension awoke ~1 hour ago with sudden left-arm paralysis, left facial tingling, dysarthria, and mild dysphagia—high suspicion for acute cerebrovascular accident; emergency ambulance arranged.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Inability to move left arm on awakening today (~1 hour before call).  
• Course: Symptoms abrupt on waking; persistent and unchanged during call.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Tingling on left side of face since onset.  
  – Difficulty swallowing liquids; slight spillage noted.  
  – Speech feels slower/more effortful (dysarthria).  
  – No pain, no discoloration, and no coldness in the arm.  
  – No left-leg symptoms.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: None identified; patient slept in usual position.  
• Review of systems (pertinent negatives): No prior similar episodes; no reported headache, visual loss, chest pain, or shortness of breath.  

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus.  
• Hypertension.  
Medications (patient-reported):  
  – Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – Losartan – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  – Amlodipine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
Allergies: Penicillin (reaction details not stated).

Social History:
• Lives alone.  
• Former smoker (quantity/quit date not specified).  
• Alcohol: “A few” pints of beer on weekends plus a couple during the week.  
• No illicit drug use mentioned.

Family History:
• Father with heart disease (details unknown).  
• No other familial illnesses reported.

Physical Examination:
(Telephone consultation – no direct examination)  
Patient-reported findings:  
• Complete motor loss in left arm.  
• Left facial tingling.  
• Dysarthria and mild dysphagia.

Investigations:
• None performed prior to ambulance dispatch.

Assessment & Plan:
Issue 1: Suspected acute ischemic stroke vs. other cerebrovascular event  
  – Sudden focal neurological deficit (left-arm paralysis, facial tingling, dysarthria, dysphagia) within 1 hour of onset.  
Plan:  
  • Emergency ambulance called to transport patient to nearest Emergency Department/stroke unit.  
  • Advise patient to unlock front door and wait in hallway for paramedics.  
  • GP remained on the phone until ambulance arrival.  
  • Anticipate in-hospital stroke protocol: rapid neuro-imaging and consideration of thrombolysis/thrombectomy.

Issue 2: Cardiometabolic risk factors (type 2 diabetes, hypertension)  
  – Contribute to stroke risk; long-term management to be revisited after acute event.  
Plan:  
  • Document current medications; confirm adherence and efficacy during post-hospital follow-up.  
  • Review blood pressure and glycemic control once clinically appropriate.

General plan items:  
• Ensure hospital receives full medical history, medication list, and penicillin allergy.  
• Arrange follow-up with primary care after discharge for secondary stroke prevention and chronic disease optimization.

Quality checks:

Missing/expected elements:  
• No vital signs obtained.  
• No medication doses, routes, or frequencies documented.  
• No comprehensive neurological exam possible via phone.  
• No laboratory/imaging data available.

Internal conflicts: None noted in transcript.

Transcript quality: Clear; no significant background noise; complete answers obtained.
